subtopics.title: Number Scales on the Country's Road Map

questions.question: On a 1 : 2 000 000 map, one centimetre on paper represents:
The N3 route measures 28,5 cm on the 1 : 2 000 000 map. The real distance is:
Bloemfontein is about 300 km from Pretoria by road. On this map that is:
options: 15 cm — ground to paper shrinks, so divide by 20

questions.question: The map answer of 570 km against the signposted 568 km shows that:
options: The map is wrong and should not be used
Scales only work for short distances
Map measurement is honest estimation — the memo allows a small range for ruler accuracy

subtopics.title: Bar Scales and Making a Scale of Your Own

questions.question: A bar scale segment is 2 cm long and labelled 50 km. A road measuring 7 cm is:
options: 175 km — each centimetre is worth 25 km

questions.question: After photocopying a map at a reduced size:
options: The bar scale stays true because it shrank with the roads; the printed ratio becomes a lie
The number scale stays true; the bar scale fails

questions.question: A bakkie is really 4,5 m long and its drawing is 9 cm. The scale of the drawing is:
options: 1 : 50 — because 9 : 450 in the same units simplifies to 1 : 50

questions.question: A 30 m hall must be modelled on an 80 cm display board. The most suitable scale is:
options: 1 : 50, giving a 60 cm model — as large as the space allows while still fitting

questions.question: The index entry 'Harrismith, D3' means the town is found:
options: In the block where column D crosses row 3 — the grid names a block, not a pinpoint
At the corner of the map

questions.question: From Johannesburg, Durban lies to the:
options: South-east — down and right on the page

questions.question: Johannesburg as seen FROM Durban lies to the:
options: North-west — swapping the towns reverses the direction

questions.question: A distance table beats ruler-and-scale for trip planning because:
options: Tables are easier to read than rulers
The ruler cannot measure long roads
The table gives ROAD kilometres, while the ruler takes a straight line your wheels cannot take

subtopics.title: Slope on Maps: Contours and Gradient

questions.question: With a contour interval of 20 m, a path crossing five contour lines has climbed:
options: 100 m — five crossings times 20 m each

questions.question: Contours packed close together on a map mean:
options: Steep ground — the height changes quickly over a short distance

questions.question: A path rises 100 m while covering 2 000 m horizontally. Its gradient is:
options: 1 : 20 — for every 20 m forward, 1 m up

questions.question: Comparing gradients of 1 : 5 and 1 : 20:
options: Neither can be compared without the map
1 : 5 is steeper — the smaller second number packs the same climb into less distance

questions.question: The 'one clever move' before touching the ruler is:
options: Working out what one centimetre is worth — 1 : 2 000 000 means every centimetre is 20 km

questions.question: A map answer of thousands of centimetres for a page distance signals that:
options: You multiplied where you should have divided — the sense test catches it

questions.question: When the map is zoomed on a phone screen, you should trust:
options: The striped bar — it grew along with the roads, so its promise still holds

subtopics.title: Where It Is and Which Way It Lies

questions.question: To find Harrismith from the index entry D3, you:
options: Run down column D, across row 3, and search only that block with your eyes

questions.question: Driving SOUTH down the N3, the Midlands are on your right. Driving home NORTH in January, the same hills are:
options: On your LEFT — body directions travel with you; the hills did not move, you turned around

questions.question: The two 'languages' of direction are:
options: Compass words fixed by the world, and body words — left, right, straight — that travel with the traveller

questions.question: The ruler's straight line between two towns is always:
options: Shorter than the road distance — the table knows the bends

subtopics.title: Reading the Hills Without Climbing Them

questions.question: Each brown contour line on the trail map joins:
options: All ground at the SAME height — walk along it and you stay level
The steepest points of the mountain
The start and end of the path

questions.question: Two paths cross the same five contour lines; one does it in a thumb of map, the other in a full hand. The steeper path is:
options: The thumb path — the same climb squeezed into less walking
Neither, since they cross the same lines

questions.question: As ladders against a wall, gradients 1 : 5 and 1 : 20 look like:
options: The 1 : 5 ladder standing nearly upright and the 1 : 20 leaning gently

questions.question: A 6 km path at a walking pace of 4 km/h takes:
options: 90 minutes — 6 ÷ 4 = 1,5 hours, before juice stops and steep sections
